diagnosis: No progress is happening because the incumbent is a jammed LP fixed point: it has roughly 450 contacts tied at slack $10^{-16}$--$10^{-14}$, versus only $3\cdot153-6=453$ effective degrees of freedom on $(S^3)^{153}$ modulo rotations, so almost every linearized feasible direction is blocked. Yet it has one zero-contact rattler, meaning the other 152 points form an essentially isostatic, saturated subsystem while the rattler sits in a hole too small for it; lowering the maximum requires a collective rearrangement that breaks many contacts at once to make room for that point, not a tangent-space move. The workers so far use Gaussian kicks around a single incumbent followed by softmax descent and greedy LP polishing, so small kicks fall back to the same contact graph and large kicks are polished to worse optima and discarded. The missing structural property is a balanced, fully locked configuration—ideally with some symmetry or near-symmetry—in which every point carries comparable contact load and the slack is shared by all 153 points rather than concentrated in a jammed 152-point core plus a spare point.

diagnosis: All evaluated programs return the record basin, whose fingerprint is visible in the plots: roughly 460 pairs are tied at the maximum to within $10^{-14}$, followed by a large gap to the next pair at slack $\sim 10^{-5}$--$10^{-4}$. One point is a rattler with 0 contacts while the other 152 points carry 4--8 contacts each, so the non-rattler core is already first-order rigid and LP polishing can only re-equalize the same contacts. Single-point moves of the rattler, and the small-to-moderate random kicks tried so far, cannot lower the core's maximum; any improvement must move many core points cooperatively while a contact is broken and a second-shell pair becomes a contact instead. The missing structural property is thus a fully jammed, load-balanced configuration: no wasted point, more uniform contact counts, and a different contact graph in which the rattler's slack is redistributed across the whole code.

diagnosis: The plots show about 460 pairs tied at the maximum cosine to within $10^{-12}$, with the next shell only about $10^{-5}$ away, so almost any displacement immediately creates a new blocking contact. One point is a 0-contact rattler while many others have 7-8 contacts, meaning 152 points carry roughly 460 contacts against only $152\cdot3-6=450$ effective degrees of freedom and are over-jammed, while the rattler's 3 degrees of freedom are wasted. Hence the trust-region LP has no feasible improving direction, small kicks plus soft-max annealing relax back to the same contact graph, and large kicks are rejected as worse before they can find another graph. The missing structural property is a balanced, rattler-free, near-isostatic contact graph in which every point, including the present rattler, has roughly 3-6 contacts and no hub is heavily over-pinned.

diagnosis: After 60 programs the gain is only $1.85\times10^{-8}$, because repeated annealing plus LP polishing from the same incumbent keeps returning to the same basin. The image shows roughly 450 contacts tied at slack below $10^{-9}$, followed by a clear gap to the next pairs, while 153 points on $S^3$ have only $153\cdot3-6=453$ effective degrees of freedom, so the configuration is essentially rigidly jammed. Yet its contact degrees are highly uneven, ranging from an under-braced 2-contact point to several 8-contact hubs, with no visible symmetry or regular organisation in the projected contact graph. The missing structural property is therefore a balanced, stress-equilibrated, approximately isostatic contact graph in which every point is locked by comparably loaded contacts, rather than this heterogeneous jam produced by local minimax squeezing.
